title: Moon Transfer 101: From LEO to Lunar Surface
excerpt: How a translunar injection burn, 3-day coast, and lunar orbit insertion add up to a crewed Moon landing.
body:
# Moon Transfer 101

A crewed Moon mission is not a single burn — it's a chain of maneuvers each with its own margin.

## 1. Launch to LEO
Your rocket puts the stack into a circular low-Earth orbit (~200–400 km). From there the real journey begins.

## 2. Trans-Lunar Injection (TLI)
A ~3.1 km/s burn raises apogee to the Moon's distance. The spacecraft then coasts for ~3.2 days along a highly elliptical orbit.

## 3. Lunar Orbit Insertion (LOI)
At perilune, a ~0.9 km/s retrograde burn captures into low lunar orbit.

## 4. Descent & Landing
The lander separates, descends, and touches down. Total surface Δv budget ~2.0 km/s.

## Δv Summary (Apollo-style)
| Maneuver | Δv (km/s) |
|----------|-----------|
| TLI | 3.10 |
| LOI | 0.90 |
| Descent | 2.00 |
| **Total** | **~6.0** |

The Mission Planner on this site computes these numbers from your selected launch vehicle and payload.

title: Mars Launch Windows: Why Every 26 Months?
excerpt: The geometry of Earth and Mars orbits creates a ~780-day cycle — here's why and what it means for mission mass.
body:
# Mars Launch Windows Explained

Earth laps Mars every **779.94 days** (the synodic period). This is the rhythm of interplanetary exploration.

## The Geometry
- Earth orbital period: 365.25 days
- Mars orbital period: 686.98 days
- Relative angular speed: 360°/365.25 − 360°/686.98 ≈ 0.461°/day
- Time to gain 360°: 360 / 0.461 ≈ 780 days

## Hohmann Transfer to Mars
The minimum-energy trajectory departs at Earth-Mars opposition + ~44° phase angle. Transfer time ~259 days.

## Why It Matters for Mass
Outside the window, Δv increases sharply. The Mission Planner shows how your launch vehicle's payload capacity drops as the departure date drifts from the optimal window.

## Next Windows (Earth→Mars)
| Launch Opens | Launch Closes | Arrival |
|--------------|---------------|---------|
| Late 2026 | Early 2027 | Late 2027 |
| Late 2028 | Early 2029 | Late 2029 |
| Late 2030 | Early 2031 | Late 2031 |

Plan early — habitat mass, radiation shielding, and consumables all scale with transit time.

title: Radiation Budgets for Deep-Space Crew
excerpt: Galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events set the real limit on mission duration — here's the math.
body:
# Radiation Budgets for Deep-Space Crew

Space radiation comes in two flavors:

## Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR)
High-energy nuclei (mostly H, He, Fe) — isotropic, continuous, hard to shield. Typical deep-space dose rate: **0.5–1.0 mSv/day** behind modest aluminum shielding.

## Solar Particle Events (SPE)
Bursts of protons from solar flares — directional, sporadic, potentially lethal without a storm shelter. A large SPE can deliver **>1000 mSv** in hours to an unshielded crew.

## NASA Career Limits
| Age / Sex | Limit (mSv) |
|-----------|-------------|
| 30-yo male | 800 |
| 30-yo female | 600 |
| 50-yo male | 1200 |

## Shielding Trade-offs
- **Water / polyethylene**: best mass efficiency for GCR (~15 g/cm² halves dose)
- **Storm shelter**: dedicated small volume (e.g., 5 g/cm²) for SPE events
- **Active shielding** (magnetic/electric): promising but TRL 3–4

The Life Support core in this app computes mission radiation dose from transit + surface days and compares to the career limit for your crew profile.

title: Farmer Persona Sky Card — A Deep Dive
excerpt: How the Cosmic Data Commons turns almanac data into planting-day decisions for a mid-latitude farmer.
body:
# Farmer Persona Sky Card — A Deep Dive

The Farmer card answers: **"When should I plant?"**

## Signals Computed
1. **Day length & sun path** — photoperiod for crop variety selection
2. **Moon phase** — traditional planting lore (root crops at new moon, leaf at full)
3. **Tidal window** — high/low tide times for coastal fields
4. **Solunar periods** — major/minor feeding times (fish & wildlife activity)
5. **Insolation index** — clear-sky daily MJ/m² scaled by cloud climatology
6. **Frost window** — median last-freeze / first-freeze dates for the latitude
7. **Meteor shower proximity** — nights of elevated fire risk (dry conditions + fireballs)

## Live Feeds (when online)
- **Solar flux (F10.7)** → ionospheric absorption → GPS precision for auto-steer tractors
- **Kp index** → GNSS scintillation risk → RTK correction reliability
- **Aurora oval** → high-latitude comms degradation

## Offline Mode
All almanac signals (1–7) are computed from the JPL DE440 ephemeris and NOAA solar algorithms — no network required. The farmer gets a complete briefing even in a cornfield with zero bars.

title: Communications Delay & Relay Architecture for Mars
excerpt: From 4 to 24 minutes one-way — how missions plan around the speed of light.
body:
# Communications Delay & Relay Architecture for Mars

Light is fast. Space is big. The combination means **no real-time control**.

## Earth–Mars Light Time
| Geometry | One-way | Round-trip |
|----------|---------|------------|
| Closest approach (opposition) | 3.0 min | 6.0 min |
| Conjunction (Sun in between) | 22.3 min | 44.6 min |
| Typical transfer midpoint | 12–15 min | 24–30 min |

## Relay Assets
- **MRO / MAVEN / TGO / MEX** — UHF relay orbiters (250–400 km altitude)
- **DSN 34 m / 70 m** — Earth ground stations (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra)
- **Future**: Mars Relay Network (MRN) — dedicated comm satellites

## Operational Impact
- **Rover drives**: planned sol-by-sol, not joystick
- **Science decisions**: uplink overnight, downlink next morning
- **Emergency**: crewed missions need onboard autonomy for aborts

The Live Frontier ribbon shows Voyager's current light-lag as a reference — Mars is ~100× closer than Voyager 1, but the ops discipline is the same.

title: Apollo 11 Replay: The 3-Day Coast to the Moon
excerpt: Relive the translunar coast — TLI, mid-course corrections, LOI, and the view from the command module.
body:
# Apollo 11 Replay

**Launch**: 1969-07-16 13:32 UTC from KSC LC-39A (Saturn V SA-506).

## Timeline
| Event | GET (hh:mm:ss) | UTC |
|-------|----------------|-----|
| Launch | 00:00:00 | 1969-07-16 13:32:00 |
| TLI ignition | 02:44:16 | 1969-07-16 16:16:16 |
| TLI cutoff | 02:50:03 | 1969-07-16 16:22:03 |
| CSM/LM separation | 03:17:04 | 1969-07-16 16:49:04 |
| MCC-1 (mid-course) | 26:44:58 | 1969-07-17 16:16:58 |
| MCC-2 | 61:40:00 | 1969-07-19 01:12:00 |
| LOI-1 ignition | 75:49:50 | 1969-07-19 15:21:50 |
| LOI-2 | 80:11:36 | 1969-07-19 19:43:36 |
| Undocking (LM) | 100:12:00 | 1969-07-20 17:44:00 |
| Powered descent | 102:33:05 | 1969-07-20 20:05:05 |
| **Touchdown** | **102:45:40** | **1969-07-20 20:17:40** |

## The View
During the 3-day coast, the Earth shrank from a disk filling the window to a marble. The Moon grew from a sliver to a dominant presence. The Fly view in this app recreates that coast with the real trajectory.

## Your Turn
Open **Fly** → select **Apollo 11** → scrub the timeline. Watch the TLI burn, the coast, and the lunar approach.
